analysis.one_liner: Shifts plastic and packaging waste costs onto producers and phases out many single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make companies that make and sell packaged products pay for collecting, recycling, and composting them after use, create a national 10-cent deposit on beverage containers that consumers get back when they return the container, and phase out items like plastic bags, utensils, and foam food containers. It would also temporarily stop approval of new or expanded plastics manufacturing plants until pollution rules are updated, require recycled content in plastic bottles, standardize recycling labels nationwide, and restrict exports of plastic waste to other countries.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households gain in several ways: every beverage container carries a refundable deposit (at least 10 cents) that comes back to the person who returns it, curbside and drop-off recycling becomes more convenient and uniform nationwide, and honest labeling ends the practice of marking unrecyclable items with the recycling symbol. Cities, counties, and taxpayers gain because producers, not local governments, must fund collection, litter cleanup from public places and waterways, and upgrades to recycling infrastructure. Communities near plastics plants gain from a pause on new plant permits until pollution rules catch up.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, local taxpayers, and communities near plastics plants

how_it_helps.text: Producers of packaging, paper, single-use products, and beverages must join producer responsibility organizations and pay the costs of collecting, transporting, recycling, composting, and cleaning up their products after consumer use, including litter from public places and marine environments.

A national beverage container deposit of at least 10 cents must be charged to consumers and refunded on return; deposits on unreturned containers go into collection and recycling infrastructure, and retailers must accept returns of any brand during business hours.

Beginning January 1, 2022, covered establishments may not provide single-use plastic carryout bags or plastic utensils; straws are available only on request (but must remain stocked for customers who ask), and the EPA must ban other non-recyclable single-use items like foam food service products and hotel mini-bottles.
The bill places a moratorium on new or expanded permits for facilities that manufacture plastics until regulations addressing pollution from those facilities are updated.

Plastic beverage containers must contain rising shares of US post-consumer recycled content (25% by 2025, 80% by 2040), and the EPA must set national standards for recycling labels so unrecyclable products cannot display the recycling symbol.

Organizations running the programs must dedicate at least 50 percent of their first 10 years of spending to building new US recycling and composting infrastructure, at least 10 percent to litter cleanup, and cannot charge households for collection; the bill also limits exports of plastic waste to other countries.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer product brands, beverage companies, bottlers, and packaging manufacturers pay program fees covering the full life-cycle costs of their products, plus civil penalties up to $70,117 per day for noncompliance. Large retailers take on duties to accept container returns, stop giving out banned items, and face escalating fines from $250 to $1,000 for repeat violations. Businesses under $1 million in annual revenue are exempt from the producer responsibility program, and bag-ban penalties are limited for them, but many smaller food-service and retail businesses still bear compliance and switching costs. Some of these costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices, and unclaimed deposits effectively fund the system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage, packaging, and plastics makers; large retailers

drawbacks.text: Producer responsibility fees, recycled-content mandates, and higher-material costs would likely raise shelf prices, and low-income households that buy beverages but do not redeem deposits effectively pay into the system without getting money back.
The bill exempts companies carrying out approved plans from the antitrust laws, letting competitors jointly design and fund their compliance plans without standard competition-law scrutiny.
Retailers, especially smaller ones, must handle container returns during all business hours and could be fined for violations; restaurants and small stores have some limits but still bear new duties.

A single national standard preempts the patchwork of state and local rules some communities have already tailored, and plastic straw and utensil bans add switching costs for food-service businesses, though the bill preserves on-request access for people with disabilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: shifting waste-management costs from taxpayers to the companies that design and sell packaging is a large, lasting benefit to households and local governments, and the deposit system turns waste into money back in consumers' hands. The honest objections are regressive frictions (unredeemed deposits fall hardest on people who don't return containers), price pass-through, and the antitrust exemption, which is a genuine design concession to the affected industries. On balance the design is coherent and the exemptions for very small businesses soften the worst burdens, but the compliance costs are substantial and would be felt in prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the bill on February 11, 2020, joined by 10 Senate cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics manufacturers, packaging and consumer brands, and beverage companies avoided new producer fees, a national container deposit, recycled-content mandates, and a moratorium on new plastics plant permits; local taxpayers continued bearing waste and litter costs.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shift producer responsibility for plastic waste and phase out single-use plastics.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Plastics and petrochemical industry
against.role: Industry whose products and plant buildout the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, which would have imposed producer fees, recycled-content mandates, and a moratorium on new and expanded plastics plant permits.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill freezes new and expanded plastics plant permits until EPA pollution rules are updated and phases out single-use plastic products, directly curbing the industry's growth and product lines. The industry's interest in continuing single-use plastic production runs against the public's interest in less plastic waste and pollution.

Beverage companies must charge and refund a national deposit of at least 10 cents per container, pay producer responsibility fees, and meet rising recycled-content requirements in plastic bottles. Unredeemed deposits and fees fund recycling infrastructure, converting a cost the public currently bears into an industry cost.

Brands must join producer responsibility organizations and pay the full cost of collecting, recycling, composting, and cleaning up their packaging and products, plus meet design-for-environment and truthful-labeling rules that end fake recycling symbols. Their interest in low-cost throwaway packaging runs against the public's interest in waste reduction.

industries.industry: Waste collection, recycling, and composting industry
industries.note: The bill routes producer fees through collection providers, recyclers, and composters, requiring organizations to reimburse 100 percent of collection and processing costs and to spend at least half of first-decade program funds building US recycling and composting infrastructure. The industry's revenue grows directly with the public benefit of better recycling.

Covered establishments must stop handing out banned single-use items, accept beverage container returns during business hours, and face escalating fines for repeat violations, though businesses under $1 million in revenue get partial exemptions and penalty limits. Retailers share the public's interest in less litter but bear new operating duties.
